Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A sheriff's deputy who killed six young people at a house party in Crandon, Wisconsin, apparently died after shooting himself three times in the head with a .40-caliber pistol, the state attorney general said. Tyler Peterson, a sheriff's deputy, shot and killed six people, police said. Initial reports that 20-year-old Tyler Peterson was killed by a police sniper's bullet were apparently incorrect, though it appears the sniper may have shot Peterson in the arm, Attorney General J.B. Van Hollen said. Although the final forensic determination could take several weeks, the attorney general said that Peterson had his personal .40-caliber Glock when police found him. The three gunshots to the head came from a .40-caliber. "The three gunshot wounds to the head included two nonfatal rounds with entry points below the chin, and one fatal shot that entered Peterson through the right side of the head," Van Hollen said. "Each of the three head shots were fired while the gun was in contact with his skin, or extremely close to the skin," he said. "These three head wounds are consistent with self-inflicted wounds, and not consistent with long-range rifle fire." The fourth gunshot wound, Van Hollen said, struck Peterson in the left bicep and appeared to have been fired from a rifle "at some distance."  Watch Van Hollen explain the shootings "will never make sense" » . Peterson was a Forest County sheriff's deputy and a part-time officer with the Crandon Police Department. According to Van Hollen, Peterson, while off-duty shortly before 3 a.m. Sunday, entered a house where the seven young men and women had gathered. While there, Van Hollen said, Peterson apparently got into an argument with Jordanne Murray, accusing her of having a relationship with another person. "The argument got heated, and Murray demanded he leave," the attorney general said. "Peterson left, and returned minutes later," breaking down the door and opening fire with an AR-15 rifle, of the type he was issued by the Forest County Sheriff's Department. Police said Peterson fired about 30 rounds. Fewer than 20 minutes later, a patrolling Crandon police officer, after hearing gunfire, reported it and went to the house to investigate, Van Hollen said. The officer, Greg Carter, 21, reported seeing Peterson leave the house with a rifle. After momentarily losing sight of Peterson, Carter "heard multiple rounds of gunfire" and his windshield burst. Peterson escaped. Van Hollen said that Peterson apparently "drove aimlessly around the northern part of the state" for several hours, calling in false reports to police to throw them off. Peterson  ended up at a cabin in the town of Argonne shortly before 8 a.m. He told friends about the shootings, handed over the AR-15 and two other rifles and left the cabin. After meeting with family members, he returned to the cabin around 9:15 a.m. Police arrived about 15 minutes later, Van Hollen said. Peterson was killed during a police shootout after police couldn't persuade him to surrender. All seven victims were students or graduates of Crandon High School, from which Peterson also was a graduate. In addition to Murray, the dead were identified as Aaron Smith, Bradley Schultz, Lindsey Stahl, Lianna Thomas and Katrina McCorkle. The sole survivor, Charlie Neitzel, 21, "played dead" after Peterson shot him three times, Van Hollen said. After Peterson shot him once, Neitzel begged him to stop. But Peterson fired again. Neitzel fell to the floor, was shot a third time and didn't move. "Playing dead until Peterson left, Neitzel survived," Van Hollen said. Neitzel was the last person shot. Neitzel underwent surgery Tuesday and was in stable condition Tuesday night, a hospital employee said. The families of the six slain young people asked that media leave them alone in their grief, Van Hollen told reporters. But the families of the victims also wanted it known that they had met with Peterson's family. "They hold no animosity toward them," Van Hollen said, conveying the families' wishes that the Peterson family be allowed space and time to heal. E-mail to a friend .

(CNN) — Wisconsin Attorney General J.B. Van Hollen said a sheriff’s deputy who fatally shot six young people at a house party in Crandon appears to have died after firing three shots into his own head with a .40-caliber handgun.

Police identified the gunman as 20-year-old Tyler Peterson, a Forest County sheriff’s deputy who also worked part time for the Crandon Police Department. Early accounts indicating that a police sniper had killed Peterson were apparently mistaken, although the sniper may have wounded him in the arm, Van Hollen said.

A final forensic conclusion could take several weeks. However, Peterson was found with his personal .40-caliber Glock, and the three bullets that struck his head were fired from a weapon of that caliber.

According to Van Hollen, two of the head wounds entered beneath Peterson’s chin and were not fatal. The third, fatal bullet entered through the right side of his head. All three shots were fired with the weapon touching his skin or held extremely close to it, he said.

Van Hollen said the wounds matched self-inflicted gunfire and were inconsistent with shots from a rifle at long range. A fourth bullet hit Peterson’s left bicep and appeared to have been fired from some distance with a rifle.

Van Hollen said the shootings “will never make sense.”

Shortly before 3 a.m. Sunday, while off duty, Peterson went into a home where seven young men and women were gathered. Van Hollen said Peterson apparently argued with Jordanne Murray and accused her of being involved with someone else.

As the dispute intensified, Murray ordered Peterson to leave. He did so but returned a few minutes later, forced his way through the door and began shooting with an AR-15 rifle of the type issued to him by the Forest County Sheriff’s Department. Authorities said he fired approximately 30 rounds.

Less than 20 minutes later, 21-year-old Crandon police officer Greg Carter, who was on patrol, heard the gunfire, reported it and went to investigate. Carter saw Peterson leaving the home carrying a rifle, Van Hollen said. After briefly losing sight of him, Carter heard several shots, and his windshield shattered. Peterson then escaped.

For the next several hours, Peterson apparently drove without a clear destination through northern Wisconsin. Van Hollen said he also made false reports to police in an effort to mislead investigators.

Shortly before 8 a.m., Peterson reached a cabin in the town of Argonne. He told friends about the killings, gave them the AR-15 and two additional rifles, and left. After meeting relatives, he returned to the cabin at about 9:15 a.m. Police arrived roughly 15 minutes afterward.

Authorities were unable to convince Peterson to surrender, and he died during the resulting exchange of gunfire with police. Evidence later indicated that his fatal wound was self-inflicted.

Peterson and all seven victims were either students or graduates of Crandon High School. The six people killed were Murray, Aaron Smith, Bradley Schultz, Lindsey Stahl, Lianna Thomas and Katrina McCorkle.

The only survivor, 21-year-old Charlie Neitzel, lived by pretending to be dead after Peterson shot him three times, Van Hollen said. After the first shot, Neitzel pleaded with Peterson to stop, but Peterson fired a second time. Neitzel fell to the floor, was struck by a third bullet and remained motionless until Peterson departed. He was the final person shot.

Neitzel underwent surgery Tuesday and was listed in stable condition that night, according to a hospital employee.

The families of the six people who died asked the news media to respect their privacy while they mourned, Van Hollen told reporters. They also wanted the public to know that they had met with Peterson’s relatives and did not blame or resent them. Van Hollen said the victims’ families wanted Peterson’s family to be given the privacy and time needed to recover as well.

# Off-duty deputy kills six at Wisconsin house party, wounds seventh before dying after police confrontation

**CRANDON, Wisconsin (October 8, 2007)** — An off-duty sheriff’s deputy and part-time police officer opened fire at a house party early Sunday, killing six young people and critically wounding another before fleeing and later dying after a confrontation with law enforcement, authorities said.

The gunman, identified as 20-year-old **Tyler James Peterson**, used a department-issued AR-15-style rifle in the attack, according to investigators. Peterson served as a Forest County sheriff’s deputy and as a part-time officer with the Crandon Police Department.

The shooting erupted shortly before 3 a.m. inside a home in Crandon, a small community in northern Wisconsin. Authorities said Peterson had gone to the gathering and became involved in an argument, reportedly connected to a former girlfriend.

The six people killed were **Bradley Schultz, 20; Aaron Smith, 20; Katrina McCorkle, 18; Amelia Walder, 18; Alana Walters, 18; and Lindsey Stahl, 14**.

A seventh victim, **Charlie Neitzel**, was shot and seriously wounded. He survived and was taken to a hospital for treatment.

Peterson left the scene after the gunfire, triggering a large search involving local officers, sheriff’s deputies and state and federal authorities. Schools were closed, roads were blocked, and residents were told to remain cautious as heavily armed officers searched the surrounding area.

Investigators said Peterson later contacted members of his family and acknowledged responsibility for the killings. Police eventually located him at a residence outside Crandon.

A confrontation followed in which Peterson exchanged gunfire with officers. Authorities said he was struck by police fire but ultimately died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. One law-enforcement officer was also wounded during the confrontation but survived.

Officials said Peterson’s position in law enforcement complicated the initial response because he had police training, access to a powerful weapon and familiarity with local procedures. Investigators worked to reconstruct how he obtained the rifle, what led to the argument and whether there had been warning signs before the attack.

The killings devastated Crandon, a close-knit city of about 2,000 people where many residents knew the victims, Peterson or both. Grief counselors were made available, and community members gathered for vigils as officials urged the public to support the victims’ families.

Authorities said there was no indication that another gunman was involved and that the immediate threat ended with Peterson’s death. The investigation continued as police processed the house, examined weapons and ammunition, interviewed witnesses and reviewed Peterson’s actions before and after the shooting.
